title: Lymphoplasmacyte-rich meningioma: A rare histologic variant of benign meningioma with atypical bone invasion
case_prompt:
A 57-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented after several falls without head trauma. Neurologic examination revealed moderate left hemiparesis (grade 3 on the Medical Research Council scale) without sensory deficits or cranial nerve abnormalities. Routine laboratory tests, chest radiography, and electrocardiography were unremarkable.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed a bilateral extra-axial frontoparietal mass measuring approximately 55 × 70 × 18 mm. The lesion was slightly hyperdense relative to cortex, caused hyperostotic reaction of the adjacent calvarium, and encased the middle third of the superior sagittal sinus. Prominent vasogenic edema of the right frontal lobe and corpus callosum was present, with sulcal effacement and ventricular buckling.

MRI demonstrated the lesion to be isointense on T1-weighted images, hypointense on T2-weighted images, lacking restricted diffusion, and showing relatively homogeneous enhancement after gadolinium. The superior sagittal sinus was occluded. The adjacent calvaria exhibited T1 and T2 hypointensity with enhancement on postcontrast fat-suppressed T1-weighted images.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Atypical or malignant meningioma was considered because the mass had “irregular margins and unclear tumor boundaries, which may resemble atypical or malignant meningiomas.” It was excluded as “there were no signs of cellular atypia or atypical lymphoid proliferation, and the Ki-67 index of the tumor was less than 1%.”  
2. Hypertrophic pachymeningitis was considered because “the en-plaque morphology of these tumors may resemble … hypertrophic pachymeningitis.”  
3. Granulomatous disease was considered because “the en-plaque morphology of these tumors may resemble … granulomatous disease.”  
4. Histiocytic tumors were considered because “the en-plaque morphology of these tumors may resemble … histiocytic tumors.”  
5. Inflammatory pseudotumor was considered because “the en-plaque morphology of these tumors may resemble … inflammatory pseudotumors.”  
6. Neurosarcoidosis was considered because “the en-plaque morphology of these tumors may resemble … neurosarcoidosis.”  
7. Lymphoma was considered because “the en-plaque morphology of these tumors may resemble … lymphoma.”  
8. All of these entities could not be reliably distinguished on imaging, “requiring histopathological, and immunohistochemical analysis to obtain a definitive diagnosis.”
